title: Kavi Karnapura
html:
Shivananda's Youngest Son

Kavi Karnapura — the poet to whom the Gaudiya Vaishnavas owe the drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya,” the list of the Lord's associates “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” and many other Sanskrit books on Sri Chaitanya — was the youngest son of Shivananda Sena, the same who year after year led the Bengali devotees to Puri. He has several names, and almost all of them he received from Mahaprabhu. The name given him at birth at the Lord's word is Paramananda Dasa; so the “Charitamrita” calls him (Antya 12.45, 49), and so he signs himself: “I, who bear the name Sri Paramananda Dasa” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 5), “the poet Paramananda Dasa, favoured by Srinatha, the son of Shivananda Sena” (prologue of the “Chaitanya-chandrodaya”). Yet in jest the Lord called the boy Puri Dasa (Antya 12.49; 16.65, 73), and the name speaks for itself: “the servant of Puri,” that is, of Paramananda Puri, the Lord's senior companion. Not for nothing, in Karnapura's drama Mahaprabhu, seeing Shivananda's youngest son, says to Paramananda Puri: “Svami, this is your servant.” In the list of the branches of the Chaitanya tree Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls him Karnapura (Adi 10.62), and elsewhere Kavi Karnapura (Madhya 19.118; Antya 6.262). In his great poem on Sri Chaitanya the author speaks of himself simply as the “youngest child” of Shivananda Sena (20.46). The biographies also call him Srila Kavi Karnapura Gosvami and Paramananda Sena.1

His father, Shivananda Sena, was among the great devotees of Mahaprabhu, and the son recalls him more than once in his books. In the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika,” after the bows to the Lord and His associates and the bow to the guru, there at once follows a bow to the father:

“With supreme devotion I worship my father, Sri Shivananda, the lamp of the Sena family, foremost among the associates of Mahaprabhu.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 4)

In the same book he quotes his father's words — a verse on Nityananda that he would recite as he danced (GGD 63) — and his father's opinion about Saranga Thakura: some consider Saranga to be Prahlada, “but my father does not accept this” (GGD 172).

Shivananda's sons were three: Chaitanya Dasa, Ramadasa and the youngest, Paramananda, the future Kavi Karnapura. The “Charitamrita” says of all three:

“Chaitanya Dasa, Ramadasa and Karnapura, the three sons of Shivananda, were heroic devotees of the Lord.” (CC, Adi 10.62)

“Heroic,” “valiant devotees” — in the Bengali text bhakta-shura.2 Who his elder brothers are in the eternal pastimes, Karnapura reveals himself: the two famous parrots of Vrindavana, Daksha and Vichakshana, “have now been born as my elder brothers, Chaitanya and Ramadasa” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 145). All three are glorified also in the “Vaishnava-vandana” of Devakinandana Dasa: “Chaitanya Dasa, Ramadasa and Karnapura — the three sons of Shivananda I will glorify generously” (2.73; the couplet is not in all manuscripts).

He was born, according to the “Anubhashya” of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati (on CC, Adi 10.62), in 1448 Shaka, that is, in 1526/27, in Kanchrapara (Kanchanapalli), near Kumarahatta (Halisahar), where Shivananda's house stood.3 The day of his appearance is not given in the sources, and it is not in the Vaishnava calendar of Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math. He was born, as the biographies say, by the blessing of Mahaprabhu Himself. Jagadananda Pandita too calls him a fellow villager: in the “Prema-vivarta” he glorifies Kavi Karnapura, “who lives in my village,” and adds that Gaura “at seven years of age made him honoured as a great poet” (8.15–16).

A Name Given Before Birth

Shivananda went to the Lord in Nilachala every year, and on one of these visits Mahaprabhu spoke to him of a son not yet born. Krishnadasa Kaviraja tells of it when Shivananda brings his three sons to the Lord (Antya 12.44). The Lord asked the name of the youngest, and the father answered: “Paramananda Dasa.” And here the earlier conversation is recalled:

“Earlier, when Shivananda had come to the Lord, Mahaprabhu had said to him, ‘The son who will be born to you this time — name him Puridasa.’” (CC, Antya 12.46–47)

The boy was then still in his mother's womb, and was born when Shivananda returned home (Antya 12.48).

“By the Lord's order they named him Paramananda Dasa, and the Lord jokingly called him Puridasa.” (CC, Antya 12.49)4

When Shivananda first showed the infant to the Lord, Mahaprabhu bestowed on him a mercy that shaped his whole life:

“When Shivananda presented that child, Mahaprabhu placed His big toe in the boy's mouth.” (CC, Antya 12.50)

This is no jest and no amusement: the “Charitamrita” says “jokingly” only of the nickname, while here it is a blessing. Later Karnapura himself confesses that his poetic gift came to him “by the mercy shown in His remnants.” Krishnadasa Kaviraja continues:

“Shivananda's good fortune is an ocean — who can reach its farther shore? The Lord calls his whole family His own.” (CC, Antya 12.51)

After His meal the Lord ordered that Shivananda's family should receive His prasada every day:

“‘As long as Shivananda's wife and sons are here, they should receive the plate of My remnants.’” (CC, Antya 12.53)

This order was carried out by the Lord's personal servant Govinda.5

Karnapura's own drama gives the same meeting in its own way. Shrikanta, the boy's cousin, reports to the Lord who has come: two sons of his uncle — these the Lord has already seen — and the youngest, who has not yet seen His beautiful feet. And the Lord, turning to Paramananda Puri, says: “Svami, this is your servant” (“Chaitanya-chandrodaya” 10.5).

“Say: Krishna!”

Years went by. Once Shivananda came with his wife to Puri for the Ratha-yatra and brought his youngest son, who was then seven years old:

“Taking his son, he came to the Lord and had the boy bow at His feet. Again and again the Lord said, ‘Say “Krishna”!’ But the boy stayed silent and would not utter the name of Krishna. Shivananda did all he could to persuade the boy, but still the boy did not say the name of Krishna.” (CC, Antya 16.66–68)

The Lord wondered:

“The Lord said, ‘I have made the whole world chant the holy name; I have made even trees and stones say the name of Krishna. Yet I could not make this boy say the name of Krishna!’ Hearing this, Svarupa Gosani said: ‘You have instructed him in the mantra of Krishna's name. Having received the mantra, he will not disclose it to anyone. He chants it silently, within, but does not speak it aloud. That, I think, is his intention.’” (CC, Antya 16.69–72)

So the child's silence turned out to be not obstinacy but faithfulness: the mantra received from the Lord Himself he kept in his heart. One of the biographies adds that the Lord rejoiced that so small a child knew this rule of the scriptures. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains in the “Anubhashya” on this verse: a mantra one has received from Sri Gurudeva loses its potency if disclosed to another — as is seen also from the story of Gadadhara Pandita. That is why Puri Dasa did not utter aloud the mantra Mahaprabhu had given him.

The Seven-Year-Old's Verse

The next day the Lord said to him: “Recite, Puri Dasa!” And the boy at once, without any preparation, composed and recited a verse:

“Glory to Hari! He is all the adornment of the girls of Vrindavana: the blue lotus at their ears, the collyrium of their eyes, the necklace of great sapphires upon their breast.” (CC, Antya 16.74)

Hari Himself is the whole adornment of the girls of Vraja, “every adornment” (akhilam mandanam), as the “Anubhashya” explains. According to the heading in the edition of the “Charitamrita,” this is the first verse of Karnapura's “Arya-shataka.”6

“He was a child of seven, who had not studied, yet he composed such a verse! Everyone was amazed.” (CC, Antya 16.75)

This episode is recalled also when one wishes to show that a great devotee (mahajana) can compose verses even as a child: the proof is the seven-year-old Karnapura and his verse in the arya metre.

Krishnadasa Kaviraja concludes the story thus:

“Such is the greatness of Chaitanya Prabhu's mercy; even Brahma and the other gods cannot find its limit.” (CC, Antya 16.76)

How much less an ordinary soul, adds one of the biographies. Not inborn talent nor early learning, but the Lord's mercy, received in infancy from His foot, made an untaught child a poet. Karnapura himself says so at the end of the drama: “By the mercy shown in His remnants my ripeness was born in the form of poetry” (“Chaitanya-chandrodaya,” closing verse 1).7

From that day, by tradition, the name Kavi Karnapura became his: the Lord Himself gave it to the boy on hearing his verse.8 The “Advaita-prakasha” says the same: “By Gaura's mercy all the shastras were revealed to the son of Shivananda Sena while still a small child. He became famous by the name Kavi Karnapura: the son of Shachi performed a pastime that amazed the world” (18.126–127).

The Guru

The mantra of Krishna's name the boy received from Mahaprabhu Himself. And yet, following the established order, he accepted initiation (diksha) from Srinatha Pandita (Srinatha Chakravarti) of Kanchrapara, the family guru of Shivananda's household. Srinatha was a disciple of Advaita Acharya and, on the Chaitanya tree, one of Advaita's sub-branches; the “Prema-vilasa” says that he studied the “Bhagavata” with Sri Advaita, installed the Deity of Krishna-raya in Kumarahatta, wrote a commentary on the “Bhagavata,” the “Chaitanya-mata-manjusha,” and that “his pupil is the poet Karnapura, son of Shivananda” (vilasa 24); so also the “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 10.62: “a disciple of Srinatha Pandita.” One of the biographies reports that Srinatha's Deities, it is said, are still worshipped in Kumarahatta or Kanchrapara.

Initiation “by custom” does not make the guru a mere formality, nor does it in the least diminish the mantra given by the Lord: so the order of succession is preserved, and Karnapura honours Srinatha as his guru. In the first verse after the invocation of the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” he bows before him:

“We bow to our guru named Srinatha, a moon in the line of the brahmanas, a jewelled ornament of the earth as it were, dear to the Lord: having tasted the pure, unalloyed talks of the secret pastimes of Vrindavana that pour from his lips, no one in the world delights in anything else.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 3)

At the end of the same book he explains why he has not named Srinatha's former name in Krishna's pastimes: the shastra forbids uttering the name of one's guru (GGD 210) — and he adds that Srinatha expounded the “Bhagavata-samhita” with skill and that his glory is Krishnadeva, who shines in Kumarahatta (GGD 211). In the prologue of the drama, too, the author is called a poet “favoured by Srinatha.” In the introduction to the “Ananda-vrindavana-champu” Karnapura likewise bows to his guru, and in another introductory verse glorifies Mahaprabhu as the family Deity who accepted Shivananda's whole family as His own — just as the “Charitamrita” says (Antya 12.51).

In Vraja

Of himself Karnapura says nothing in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika,” but he names who his parents were in Vraja:

“The messenger Vira, who once in Vrindavana led all the gopis to Krishna, is now my father; she who in Vraja was Bindumati is now my mother.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 176)

Vira is a messenger-sakhi (duti) who serves the meetings of Radha and Krishna. These are eternal companions of the Lord who descended together with Him, not souls that were “reborn.” One of the biographies concludes from this that Karnapura too is Krishna's companion in Vraja, although he kept silent about himself.

A late tradition (the “Vaishnava-achara-darpana”) calls him Gunachura-sakhi in Vraja and says that he is a branch of the Chaitanya tree, lived in Kanchrapara, and received from Mahaprabhu the name Puri Dasa and great spiritual power when the toe of the Lord's foot came into his mouth.9

Books

Almost all that is known of Karnapura after his childhood is his books. The biographies name among them the drama “Sri Chaitanya-chandrodaya-nataka,” the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika,” the “Ananda-vrindavana-champu,” the great poem on Sri Chaitanya, the treatise on poetics “Alankara-kaustubha,” a commentary on the Tenth Canto of the “Bhagavata,” and the “Arya-shataka”; one of them adds the “Brihad-ganoddesha-dipika,” the “Ahnika-kaumudi,” the “Chaitanya-sahasra-nama” and the “Keshavashtaka.” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” (on Adi 10.62) lists the “Ananda-vrindavana-champu,” the “Alankara-kaustubha,” the great poem “Sri Chaitanya-charita” (with a question mark), the “Chaitanya-chandrodaya,” the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” and other books.10

When each was written, the books themselves tell. The great poem was completed in 1464 Shaka (1542), in the month of Shuchi (Ashadha), on a Monday, on the second tithi of the dark fortnight (20.49). Of the drama Karnapura writes in its last verse: Gaura Hari appeared in 1407 Shaka, and this book in 1494 (1572). The “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” is dated 1498 Shaka (1576; GGD 215); according to the “Anubhashya,” he wrote until that year. The biographies regard the great poem as his first book.11

“Chaitanya-charita-mahakavya”

The great poem in twenty cantos is an account of the Lord written, as the author says, from what was seen and heard:

“Some things I saw myself, some I heard. To me, utterly foolish, those for whom His pastimes are life itself told of Him again and again. Some things stayed in memory here and there. Of these I, insignificant, tell a little, because His mercy leads me.” (“Chaitanya-charita-mahakavya” 1.10)

As his chief source he names the records of Murari Gupta: “whatever was written … by one who bears the auspicious name ‘Murari’ — having looked at all that, this child has written it down” (20.42); and again and again he bows to Murari, by whose mercy “the nectar of the deeds of Chaitanya-chandra was drunk with the eyes” (20.43). The signature at the end of the poem is the “youngest child” of Shivananda Sena, “the embodiment of the rasa of love for the supremely merciful Gaurachandra” (20.46).

“Chaitanya-chandrodaya”

The drama on Sri Chaitanya conveys His deeds faithfully. As befits a drama, the order of events is shifted here and there, but in the presentation of Mahaprabhu's teaching there is no deviation whatever — and for this the Gaudiya Vaishnavas revere and love this book. It begins with a prologue: at the festival of Jagannatha's procession to the Gundicha, the sutradhara, at the command of King Prataparudra, stages a drama composed by “the poet Paramananda Dasa … the son of Shivananda Sena”; the festival is the same, the same Lord of the Blue Mountain, “but all this, alas, without Mahaprabhu we hold empty” (Act 1, v. 2).12

“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika”

This book — “a lamp showing the associates of Gaura” — names who in Krishna's pastimes were those who appeared as companions and devotees at the descent of Sri Krishna Chaitanya. From the first verses the author wards off any suspicion of invention, and says himself where his knowledge comes from:

“The famous associates of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, and those of the great Nityananda and Advaita too, and some of the former names of the cowherds which the first sages — Svarupa and others — pointed out each in his own book: having studied these, and having heard others from the lips of saints living in Mathura, in Odra (Orissa) and in Gauda, having considered them with my own understanding, and being repeatedly asked by some — I, named Sri Paramananda Dasa, carrying out the command given to me, write them down.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 5)13

It also gives the guru-parampara of the Gaudiyas — from Brahma through Narada and Vyasa to Madhvacharya and onward, down to Madhavendra Puri (GGD 22); from here, it seems, Baladeva Vidyabhushana too took his list of acharyas from Madhva to Chaitanya. This book, Karnapura writes, should be kept hidden from disputants and given to those versed in the scriptures on rasa who have taken shelter of Gaura's feet (GGD 213); “this ‘Sri Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika’ has been composed by me” (GGD 214).

Many later accounts of the Lord's associates rely on it as testimony: Svarupa Damodara is Vishakha, Gadadhara Pandita is Radha, Prabodhananda is Tungavidya, Kashishvara and Govinda are Bhringara and Bhangura, Saranga is Nandimukhi, and many more. Scenes from his drama are often cited as well — for example, the Lord's seven days in Madhava's house in Kuliya, Prataparudra's valour, Rupa — and passages from the great poem.

“Ananda-vrindavana-champu” and Others

The “Ananda-vrindavana-champu” is a large book in which prose alternates with verse, in twenty-two parts. It describes Krishna's lila from the festival of Nanda (Krishna's birth) up to the rasa-lila and is so captivating that it gives the highest joy even to connoisseurs of rasa who are masters of poetry. Later Srila Vishvanatha Chakravarti wrote a commentary on it, the “Sukha-vartini,” and on the “Alankara-kaustubha” the “Subodhini”; on the “Alankara-kaustubha” there is also the commentary “Didhiti-prakashika” by Vrindavana (Tarkalankara), a disciple of Krishnadeva Sarvabhauma.

Karnapura's verses also entered the “Padyavali” of Srila Rupa Gosvami; from this it is inferred that Rupa compiled the “Padyavali” after meeting Mahaprabhu.

His Verses in the “Charitamrita”

Krishnadasa Kaviraja more than once quotes Karnapura's verses. Having told of the Lord's meeting with Rupa in Prayaga, he writes:

“Kavi-karnapura, the son of Shivananda Sena, has written at length in his book about the Lord's meeting with Rupa.” (CC, Madhya 19.118)

and quotes three verses from the ninth act of the drama (Madhya 19.119–121). Of the Lord's mercy to Sanatana, too, he speaks in the words of the “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” (Madhya 24.342–345); and Narahari Chakravarti in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” repeats: “Kavi Karnapura, dear to the Lord, wrote a book and told of the grace shown to Sanatana,” and quotes the same verses (1.657–660). And of Raghunatha Dasa Krishnadasa Kaviraja says:

“In this connection Sri Kavi-karnapura wrote of Raghunatha's glory at length in his book.” (CC, Antya 6.262)

In the drama this glorification of Raghunatha is spoken by the poet's father, Shivananda:

“Beloved by the hearts of all, he is a wondrous land of good fortune that yields its harvest without ploughing: the very moment the seed was sown in it, the incomparable tree of His love bore fruit.” (CC, Antya 6.264)

Last Years

Of Karnapura's later years we know only what he himself said in his books. In the closing verses of the drama he writes:

“As far as I could, by my own understanding, as I saw and as I heard, I, a child, by His mercy composed this account of Sri Chaitanya. Now that the circle of His beloved ones — O Shiva, Shiva! — remains only in memory, who will understand it, who will listen? So let Krishna Himself be pleased with it.” (“Chaitanya-chandrodaya,” closing verse 2)

And then follows a bitter verse of separation: “We saw the bhagavatas, received their mercy and lived among them”; while they were with us we lived — but if without them such as we cannot live anyway, why did we not depart at once, as soon as we were born? (closing verse 3). So he wrote when most of the Lord's associates had already withdrawn from sight.

Later books have preserved two more testimonies. According to the “Advaita-prakasha,” when Advaita Acharya before His disappearance called the devotees to Shantipura, there came also “the best of panditas, Kavi Karnapura” (22.106); according to the “Prema-vilasa,” he was among the branches of Mahaprabhu gathered for the memorial festival in Katwa (19.142).

When and where Kavi Karnapura departed from this world no source reports; the place of his samadhi is not known either. The last date we know is 1576, when the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” was completed. His days of appearance and disappearance are not in the Vaishnava calendar of Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

As late as the eighteenth century Narahari Chakravarti, in the “Namamrita-samudra,” his prayers to the Lord's associates, after Shivananda, Kashi Mishra and Ramananda Vasu turns to him as well:

“O Karnapura! This is what I ask of you: let me be ceaselessly immersed in the pastimes of Gauranga.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 36)

He asks for that very thing which Karnapura sang all his life.

Significance

Kavi Karnapura's books enriched the literature on Sri Chaitanya both in quality and in number. One of the biographies calls him a saint by nature and a celebrated poet; for his undivided devotion to Sri Chaitanya, his extraordinary holy life and the wealth of sweet books full of knowledge that he left to all eager to know Mahaprabhu and His teaching, his name is remembered with obeisance and reverence.14 He is a living witness of what Krishnadasa Kaviraja said: the mercy of Sri Chaitanya has no limit, and even Brahma cannot find it. The infant into whose mouth the Lord placed the toe of His foot, the boy who kept the mantra the Lord had given, became the poet who brought down to us His pastimes and the names of His eternal associates.

Notes

  1. One of the biographies calls him “Paramananda Puri (Puri Dasa for short)” and writes that the Lord told them to name the child “Paramananda.” According to the “Charitamrita,” the Lord told them to give him the name Puri Dasa, while they gave him the name Paramananda Dasa at His instruction (Antya 12.47–49); Paramananda Puri is the name of a sannyasi, the Lord's companion, after whom the boy was called “the servant of Puri.” Another biography writes that all these names — Paramananda Dasa, Paramananda Sena, Puri Dasa — were given him by his father; according to the “Charitamrita,” the names were given at the Lord's word. Kavi Karnapura should not be confused with Karnapura Kaviraja, the disciple of Srinivasa Acharya.
  2. One of the biographies applies the word bhakta-shura to one person — to him or to Shivananda (the text is unclear); in the “Charitamrita” it is said of all three sons.
  3. One of the biographies gives the year 1527 and the place as Kanchanapalli, or Kanchrapara; another names the place Kanchan-puri, near Calcutta.
  4. One of the biographies writes that the name was given “long before birth.” According to the “Charitamrita,” when the Lord said this to Shivananda, the child was already in his mother's womb (Antya 12.48).
  5. One of the biographies merges this episode with a later one: the Lord supposedly gave His toe on the same visit when the seven-year-old boy kept silent, and the boy, having bowed, began of himself to suck it. According to the “Charitamrita,” the Lord Himself placed His toe in the infant's mouth (Antya 12.50; according to another biography, in the year after his birth), while the silence and the verse came years later (Antya 16.65–75). The late tradition (the “Vaishnava-achara-darpana”) also says that the boy himself put the Lord's toe into his mouth.
  6. One of the biographies writes that the Lord asked him to recite “a verse about Krishna”; in the “Charitamrita” it is simply “Recite, Puri Dasa!” (Antya 16.73).
  7. One of the biographies puts into the mouth of Krishnadasa Kaviraja a further statement as well: the boy received the mercy “long before he saw the light of the sun,” when he sucked the toe of the Lord's foot, and from this power and learning awoke in him. The “Charitamrita” (Antya 16.76) speaks only of the boundlessness of the mercy; the rest is the biographer's interpretation, and “before the light of the sun” disagrees with Antya 12.50: the Lord gave His toe to an infant already born; before birth there was only the name.
  8. So write two biographies; one of them refers to Antya 16, but this is not there. In the “Charitamrita” the name “Karnapura” stands in the list of the branches (Adi 10.62), and “Kavi Karnapura” in Madhya 19.118 and Antya 6.262, without any account of how it was given.
  9. Karnapura himself is silent about himself, while in his “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” Gunachuda is one of the gopis, the maidservants of Radha, and by the order of the list this is Subuddhi Mishra (GGD 194–207).
  10. One of the biographies calls the great poem “Sri Chaitanya-charita-mahatmyam,” omits the “Arya-shataka” from its list though it quotes a verse from it, and writes that Karnapura “compiled” these books; only the second names the “Brihad-ganoddesha-dipika,” the “Ahnika-kaumudi,” the “Chaitanya-sahasra-nama” and the “Keshavashtaka.”
  11. If Karnapura was born in 1526/27, he finished the great poem at fifteen or sixteen. In the “Anubhashya” on Adi 10.62 Srila Bhaktisiddhanta relates the opinion of those who know that the author of the great poem is the elder brother, Chaitanya Dasa, and not Kavi Karnapura; yet the signature of the poem (20.46) is the “youngest child” of Shivananda.
  12. In the prologue of the drama King Prataparudra, already after the Lord's disappearance, commands it to be staged, while the drama itself, according to its last verse, appeared in 1572; according to historical information, Prataparudra reigned until about 1540. This discrepancy lies within the frame of the drama.
  13. One of the biographies writes that in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” the information is taken “from the words and writings of Mahaprabhu Himself” and from the writings of Svarupa Damodara and Murari Gupta. Verse 5 names the books of Svarupa and other first sages, the accounts of saints, his own reflection and requests; Gaura's words the book quotes from the “Gaura-chandrodaya” (GGD 34), Murari in verse 94, Svarupa in verses 13 and 17; “writings of Mahaprabhu” it does not mention.
  14. The word charana-kavi in the biography means here “celebrated poet,” not “wandering bard.”
